title: The MC6845 CRT controller, its registers
covers: The registers R0 to R17 of the MC6845 CRT controller: the horizontal and vertical timing, interlace, cursor, start address and light pen registers; and R18, R19 and R31 of the 6545 family, the update address registers and the dummy location that signals a transparent update

rows.text: Table 2 lists R0 as Horizontal Total, in character units, with Read No and Write Yes (the capture garbles the name; its line also lists the address register).
R0 is an 8-bit register that the processor writes.
R0 is a write-only register.
R0 is stored as the horizontal total, which determines the HS frequency by defining the HS period in character times: displayed plus non-displayed characters minus one.
A read of register 0x00 returns 0: no case of the switch names it, and the default case leaves the returned byte at its initial zero.
A read of register 0x00 returns the stored horizontal total byte.
A write that changes the value calls VGA_StartResize before storing it.
Table 2 lists R1 as Horizontal Displayed, in characters, with Read No and Write Yes (the capture garbles the name).
R1 is a 8-bit register that the processor writes.
R1 is a write-only register.
R1 is stored as the number of displayed characters per line.
A read of register 0x01 returns 0: no case of the switch names it, and the default case leaves the returned byte at its initial zero.
A read of register 0x01 returns the stored byte.
Any 8-bit number may be programmed as long as the contents of R0 are greater than the contents of R1.
A write that changes the value calls VGA_StartResize before storing it.
Table 2 lists R2 as H. Sync Position, in characters, with Read No and Write Yes (the capture garbles the name).
R2 is a 8-bit register that the processor writes.
R2 is a write-only register.
R2 is stored as the HS position, which defines the horizontal sync delay (front porch) and the horizontal scan delay (back porch).
A read of register 0x02 returns 0: no case of the switch names it, and the default case leaves the returned byte at its initial zero.
A read of register 0x02 returns the stored byte.
Raising the programmed value of R2 shifts the display on the CRT screen to the left, and lowering it shifts the display to the right.
Any 8-bit number may be programmed as long as the sum of R2 and R3 is less than R0; R2 must be greater than R1.
Table 2 lists R3 as Sync Width, with Read No and Write Yes (the capture garbles the line).
R3 is a 8-bit register that the processor writes.
R3 is a write-only register.
R3 is stored as the width of the horizontal sync (HS) pulse.
A read of register 0x03 returns 0: no case of the switch names it, and the default case leaves the returned byte at its initial zero.
The low four bits are stored as the HS width; the high four bits are the VS width on the Tandy type; other types set the VS width to 16.
A read of register 0x03 returns the stored HS width, with the stored VS width in bits 7 to 4 on the Tandy machine type.
The vertical sync pulse width is fixed at 16 scan-line times.
The HS pulse width may be programmed from 1 to 15 character clock periods, allowing compatibility with the HS pulse width specifications of many monitors.
If zero is written into this register then no HS is provided.
On the Tandy machine type the VS width is stored from bits 7 to 4 of the byte; on the other types it is set to 16.
A stored width of 0 is turned into 16 character times, in recompute_parameters and in hsync_on.
A width of 0 is stored in hsyncw, so hrend equals hrstart; the Hercules and MDA status read sets its retrace bit from hrstart to hrend inclusive.
Table 2 lists R4 as Vertical Total, in character rows, with Read No and Write Yes (the capture garbles the name).
R4 is a 7-bit register that the processor writes.
R4 is a write-only register.
R4 is stored as the integer number of character row times minus one.
A read of register 0x04 returns 0: no case of the switch names it, and the default case leaves the returned byte at its initial zero.
The Tandy machine type stores all 8 bits of the byte; the other types store its low 7 bits.
A read of register 0x04 returns the stored byte.
The frequency of VS is determined by both R4 and R5; the character row times calculated are usually an integer plus a fraction, to get exactly 50 or 60 Hz.
A write that changes the value calls VGA_StartResize before storing it.
Table 2 lists R5 as V. Total Adjust, in scan lines; the same capture line lists R6 as Vertical Displayed, in character rows; both Read No and Write Yes.
R5 is a 5-bit register that the processor writes.
R5 is a write-only register.
R5, the vertical total adjust register, is stored as a number of scan lines.
A read of register 0x05 returns 0: no case of the switch names it, and the default case leaves the returned byte at its initial zero.
The byte is stored with all 8 bits, with no mask.
A read of register 0x05 returns the stored byte.
A write that changes the value calls VGA_StartResize before storing it.
R6 is a 7-bit register that the processor writes.
R6 is a write-only register.
R6 is stored as the number of displayed character rows on the CRT screen, in character row times.
A read of register 0x06 returns 0: no case of the switch names it, and the default case leaves the returned byte at its initial zero.
The Tandy machine type stores all 8 bits of the byte; the other types store its low 7 bits.
A read of register 0x06 returns the stored byte.
Any number smaller than the contents of R4 may be programmed into R6.
A write that changes the value calls VGA_StartResize before storing it.
Table 2 lists R7 as V. Sync Position, in character rows, with Read No and Write Yes (the capture garbles the name).
R7 is a 7-bit register that the processor writes.
R7 is a write-only register.
R7 is stored as the position of vertical sync with respect to the reference, in character row times.
A read of register 0x07 returns 0: no case of the switch names it, and the default case leaves the returned byte at its initial zero.
The byte is stored with all 8 bits, with no mask.
A read of register 0x07 returns the stored byte.
Raising the programmed value of R7 shifts the display position on the CRT screen up, and lowering it shifts the display down.
Any number equal to or less than the vertical total R4 and greater than or equal to the vertical displayed R6 may be used.
Table 2 lists R8 as Interlace Mode and Skew, with Note 1, Read No and Write Yes (the capture garbles the line).
R8 is a 6-bit register that the processor writes.
R8 is a write-only register.
The MC6845 only allows control of the interlace modes, as programmed by the low order two bits of R8.
Table 3: bits 1 and 0 of R8 give Normal Sync (non-interlace) at 00, Interlace Sync at 01 and Interlace Sync and Video (bits damaged in the capture).
Note 1 of Table 2 says that the interlace is shown in Table 3.
In the normal sync mode (non-interlace) only one field is available, and each scan line is refreshed at the VS frequency, for example 50 or 60 Hz.
The two interlace modes divide the frame time between even and odd alternating fields; VS delayed by half a scan line time displaces the odd field's scan lines.
In the interlace sync mode the same information is painted in both fields, which is useful for filling in a character to enhance readability.
In the interlace sync and video mode alternating lines of the character are displayed in the even and the odd field, which doubles the given bandwidth of the CRT monitor.
Care must be taken with either interlace mode to avoid an apparent flicker effect, since the refresh time of all scan lines doubles; proper monitor design can minimize it.
For interlace operation the horizontal total R0 must be odd, that is an even number of character times (the capture damages the glyphs).
For interlace sync and video mode only, the maximum scan-line address R9 must be odd, that is an even number of scan lines.
For interlace sync and video mode only, the number programmed into the vertical displayed register R6 must be one half of the actual number required.
For interlace sync and video mode only, R10 and R11 must both be even or both odd; a full block cursor shows in both fields when R11 exceeds R9.
The byte is stored with all 8 bits; a value of 3 in its two low bits selects interlace and video, which adds m_interlace_adjust to the character height.
Besides the two low bits (3 selects interlace and video), bit 0x04 of the stored byte selects row and column addressing when a row is drawn.
Only the value 3 in the two low bits is tested (interlace and video); any other value, 1 included, takes the non-interlace adjustment in the character height.
A read of register 0x08 returns 0: no case of the switch names it, and the default case leaves the returned byte at its initial zero.
A write of register 0x08 reaches the default arm, which logs a write to an illegal index.
A write of register 0x08 reaches the default arm, which logs a write to an illegal index.
A write of register 0x08 reaches the default arm, which logs a write to an illegal index.
A read of register 0x08 logs a read from an illegal index and returns all ones.
Table 2 lists R9 as Max Scan Line Address, in scan lines, with Read No and Write Yes (the capture garbles the line).
R9 is a 5-bit register that the processor writes.
R9 is a write-only register.
R9 is stored to determine the number of scan lines per character row including the spacing, which controls the row address counter.
A read of register 0x09 returns 0: no case of the switch names it, and the default case leaves the returned byte at its initial zero.
A read of register 0x09 returns the stored byte.
The programmed value of R9 is a maximum address and is one less than the number of scan lines.
A write that changes the value calls VGA_StartResize before storing it.
Table 2 lists R10 as Cursor Start, in scan lines, with Read No and Write Yes (the capture garbles the name); its Note 2 is claimed below.
R10 is a 7-bit register that the processor writes.
R10 is a write-only register.
R10 is stored to define the start scan line and the cursor blink rate.
A read of register 0x0A returns 0: no case of the switch names it, and the default case leaves the returned byte at its initial zero.
A write stores the low six bits of the byte, so bit 6 is not kept.
A read of register 0x0A returns the stored byte.
A write stores the low six bits: the low five bits give the start scan line, and bit 6 is not kept.
Bits 5 and 6 of the cursor start register control the cursor operation as shown in Table 4.
Table 4: bits 6 and 5 give Non-Blink at 00, Cursor Non-Display at 01, Blink at 1/16 field rate at 10 and Blink at 1/32 field rate at 11.
The cursor can be up to 32 scan lines high and be placed on any scan line of the character block, as shown in Figure 15.
Non-display, display, and two blink modes (16 or 32 times the field period) are available.
Note 2 of Table 2: bit 5 of the cursor start register is used for blink period control, and bit 6 is used to select blink or no blink.
When an external blink feature on characters is required, it may be necessary to perform cursor blink externally so that both blink rates are synchronized.
An invert or non-invert cursor is easily implemented by programming the CRTC for a blinking cursor and inverting the video signal externally with an exclusive-OR gate.
A write stores the low six bits and sets the cursor enabled flag to false only when bits 6 and 5 equal 01.
A write stores the low six bits and sets the cursor enabled flag to false only when bits 6 and 5 equal 01.
A write stores the low six bits, so bit 6 is not kept, and bit 5 is tested with bit 6 for the cursor enabled flag.
Modes 10 and 11 flip the cursor state every 16 or 32 calls of update_cursor_state, made when the vertical adjust cycle ends; 00 is always on, 01 always off.
Table 2 lists R11 as Cursor End, in scan lines, with Read No and Write Yes (the capture garbles the name).
R11 is a 5-bit register that the processor writes.
R11 is a write-only register.
R11 is stored to define the last scan line of the cursor.
A read of register 0x0B returns 0: no case of the switch names it, and the default case leaves the returned byte at its initial zero.
A read of register 0x0B returns the stored byte.
Table 2 lists R12 as Start Address (H), with Read No and Write Yes; the capture line ends with 0 0, whose column meaning is unclear.
R12 and R13 form a 14-bit register pair that the processor writes.
The start address register pair is write-only.
The pair is stored as the first address output by the CRTC after vertical blanking.
The pair consists of an 8-bit low-order register, MA0-MA7, and a 6-bit high-order register, MA8-MA13.
The start address register is stored; per the document it determines which portion of the refresh RAM is displayed on the CRT screen.
Hardware scrolling by character or page may be accomplished by modifying the contents of this register.
The MCGA, Olivetti and 3270PC machine types store all 8 bits of the high register, so the pair is 16 bits wide there; the others store 14 bits.
The MCGA, Olivetti and 3270PC machine types store all 8 bits of the high register; the others store its low 6 bits; the low register stores 8 bits.
Registers 0x0C and 0x0D read 0, because device_start sets m_supports_disp_start_addr_r to false.
Reads of registers 0x0C and 0x0D return the high and low bytes of the stored start address.

rows.text: Table 2 lists R14 as Cursor (H), with Read Yes and Write Yes; the capture line ends with 0 0, whose column meaning is unclear.
R14 and R15 form a 14-bit register pair that the processor writes.
R14 and R15 form a 14-bit register pair that the processor reads.
The pair is stored; per the document it positions the cursor anywhere in the refresh RAM area, allowing hardware paging and scrolling without losing the original cursor position.
R14 is the 6-bit high-order register of the pair, MA8-MA13.
A write of register 0x0E stores all 8 bits in the high half, so the pair is 16 bits wide.
A write of register 0x0E stores all 8 bits of the byte in the high half of the cursor location.
Reads of registers 0x0E and 0x0F return the high and low bytes of the cursor location, all 8 bits of each, so the pair read is 16 bits wide.

rows.text: Table 2 lists R16 as Light Pen (H), with Read Yes and Write No; the capture line ends with 0 0, whose column meaning is unclear.
R16 and R17 form a 14-bit register pair that the processor reads.
The light pen register pair is read-only.
The pair captures the refresh address output by the CRTC on the positive edge of a pulse input to the LPSTB pin.
The pair consists of an 8-bit low-order register, MA0-MA7, and a 6-bit high-order register, MA8-MA13.
The light pen pulse is asynchronous with respect to refresh address timing, so an internal synchronizer is designed into the CRTC.
Due to delays in this circuit (Figure 5), the values of R16 and R17 need to be corrected in software.
Figure 16 shows an interrupt driven approach although a polling routine could be used.
Reads of registers 0x10 and 0x11 return the light pen value shifted right by 8 and its low byte, with no mask to 6 bits on the high byte.
A write of register 0x10 stores its low 6 bits in the high half of the light pen value, and 0x11 stores a byte in the low half.
On CGA, Olivetti, Tandy, Hercules and MDA types, writing port 0x3DC with the latch untriggered stores a beam-position light pen value; registers 0x10 and 0x11 can be written too.
A write of register 0x10 keeps 6 bits of the high half; the value computed for port 0x3DC is stored as 16 bits and read back unmasked.
A read of register 0x10 also clears the light pen latched flag.
assert_light_pen_input() arms a timer whose callback stores the get_ma address and sets the latched flag; a second overload stores a caller-supplied address and sets that flag.
Table 2 lists R17 as Light Pen (L), with Read Yes and Write No (the capture garbles the line).
R17 can be read, as Table 2 marks it Read Yes.
R17 cannot be written, as Table 2 marks it Write No.
A write of register 0x11 stores the byte in the low half of the light pen value.
A read of register 0x11 also clears the light pen latched flag.
Figure 3 lists R18 as the Update Address Register (high), at register-select code 0 1 1 0 0 1 0 (the capture reads Reg IHI).
R18 is the high register of the update address; R19 is the low register.
A write of register 0x12 reaches the default arm, which logs a write to an illegal index.
Figure 3 lists R19 as the Update Address Register (low), at register-select code 0 1 1 0 0 1 1 (the capture reads Reg ILl).
R18 and R19 together are stored as one 14-bit register, the memory address at which the next read or update will occur, for transparent address mode only.
Pair R18/R19 is straight binary if bit 2 of R8 is 0, row/column if 1 (low byte column, high byte row); the capture reads R8 as RS, R18 as R1S.
A write of 0x12 or 0x13 stores into m_update_addr whenever the variant supports transparent addressing; only the call to call_on_update_address depends on the 0x88 mode bits.
Neither case 0x12 nor case 0x13 tests MODE_ROW_COLUMN_ADDRESSING; they store 6 and 8 bits of the byte into the high and low parts of m_update_addr.
A write of register 0x13 reaches the default arm, which logs a write to an illegal index.
A write of register 0x13 reaches the default arm, which logs a write to an illegal index.
Figure 3 lists R31 as the Dummy Location, at register-select code 0 1 1 1 1 1 1 (the capture reads its name as R3l).
R31 does not drive the data bus at all when it is read.
R31 stores no data but is required to detect when transparent addressing updates occur and to set the Update Ready bit.
Whenever a read or update occurs, the update address increments automatically.
The Update Ready bit of the status register goes to 0 when R31 (read as A31 in the capture) has been read or written by the MPU.
A read of 0x1F returns 0: transparent_update is called and the function returns the byte it initialised to zero.
With the 0x88 mode bits both set, an access to 0x1F increments m_update_addr, wrapped to 14 bits, and calls call_on_update_address; it does not touch m_update_ready_bit.
In transparent_update_tick, m_update_ready_bit is set and m_update_addr incremented only when the flag is clear and the 0x88 mode bits equal 0x08.
An access to 0x1F clears m_update_ready_bit only when the variant supports transparent addressing, the 0x88 mode bits equal 0x08 and the flag is set.
An access to 0x1F increments m_update_addr only with the 0x88 mode bits both set; with them equal to 0x08 the increment is in transparent_update_tick, when the flag is clear.
A read of register 0x1F reaches the default arm, which logs a read from an illegal index, and the handler then returns all ones.
A write of register 0x1F reaches the default arm, which logs a write to an illegal index; a read logs a read from an illegal index.
